inline.s: Preface
Main Text
Note: The heading of each discourse has been added for convenient reading; it is not part of the original text.

Mind-Recollection at Three Sessions” is one of the Buddha-recitation methods of the Pure Land school. It was advocated by National Master Zhongfeng of the Yuan dynasty, and its main purpose is to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and to depart forever from the boundless sea of karma. National Master Zhongfeng wrote two works concerning the Three Sessions of Mind-Recollection: one is the “Manual of the Rites of the Three Sessions of Mind-Recollection,” used for gathering together in self-cultivation; the other is the “Liturgy of the Three Sessions of Mind-Recollection,” used for performing rites to liberate the dead, guiding departed spirits to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Both are composed of seven parts — chanting the sutras, Buddha-recitation, discourses, practice of the Way, repentance, making vows, and hymns of praise — and each session includes these seven items. This essay is an annotation of the
Liturgy of the Three Sessions of Mind-Recollection
discourse section.
[The three sessions] The times of morning, noon, and sunset. [Mind-recollection] A single mind fixed upon Amitabha Buddha, without a single straying thought.

First session rite: The discourse instructs the practitioner (including both the living and the dead) that in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is none of the host of sufferings, and that a person of the Way who would seek the road home has only to settle his own mind amid the dusts and so extinguish the deluded mind. Living beings suffer without end because of greed and desire, and greed arises from forgetting one’s own nature and letting stray thoughts run wild. To leave suffering and gain bliss and be reborn in the Pure Land, faith, vows, and practice must all be complete. Therefore the practitioner should hold deep faith and make earnest vows, and uphold the Name of Amitabha Buddha with a single mind unconfused; at the end of life he shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitabha Buddha.

Second session rite: The discourse instructs the practitioner (including both the living and the dead) that mind, Buddha, and living beings are not three and not different, and reveals the mind-only Pure Land and the self-nature Amitabha Buddha. Although the Dharma-nature is thus bright and still, yet non-arising gives rise to arising, and the fruits of karma are manifestly present. Thus living beings transmigrate through the six realms and revolve through the four modes of birth. The practitioner should therefore reveal and repent, washing away the stains of karma, increasing his roots of good, and, letting go of this retributive destiny, be reborn in the Pure Land.

[The four modes of birth] Womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. Womb-born beings take form within the mother’s womb and are then born, such as humans; egg-born beings take form within an eggshell and are then born, such as birds; moisture-born beings rely on dampness to receive their form, such as insects; transformation-born beings rely on nothing but karmic power and appear suddenly, such as the devas, the hell-dwellers, and humans of the beginning of the aeon. [Retributive destiny] The karmic cause of retribution, that is, the lifespan of a single lifetime.
Third session rite: The discourse instructs the practitioner (including both the living and the dead) on the vast merit of the six-syllable sacred name “Namo Amitabha Buddha”:
A single utterance

of the name of Amitabha Buddha can sit across and sever the six sense-roots, wiping away the heavy offenses of birth and death of eight hundred thousand myriads of kotis of aeons. It is like a clear jewel cast into muddy water; the muddy water cannot but become clear. Therefore the practitioner needs only to lift up the Buddha-name, and straightway there is no other thought. Like the great blade of Tai-e, it severs afflictions; like a great wheel of flame, it burns away ignorance. Until the mind reaches single-mindedness and the two — subject and object — are both forgotten. Thus recollecting the all-virtuous great name of Amitabha Buddha, with vow and practice both deep, the merit is never wasted; one is certain to be conceived in the lotus womb, to depart forever from the sea of karma, and to realize directly avivartika (the stage of non-retrogression), perfectly attaining the supreme bodhi (becoming a Buddha).

blocks.text: Hymn of Praise on the True Incense of Precepts and Samadhi

inline.s: The true incense of precepts and samadhi, when burned, rises straight to heaven.
This disciple, in earnest devotion, burns it in the golden censer.
In an instant the fragrant haze pervades the ten directions.
In former days Yasodhara escaped calamity and dissolved the hindrances of misfortune.
Namo to the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva of the fragrant cloud canopy
(recited three times)
[True incense of precepts and samadhi] Burning incense purifies the air, whereas the true incense of precepts and samadhi purifies the body (conduct), the mind, and the social environment. [Ruo (
ruò
)] to burn. [Yin-yun (
yīn yūn

)] to pervade. [In former days Yasodhara escaped calamity and dissolved the hindrances of misfortune] In former days Yasodhara observed the precepts and samadhi with utmost strictness. Bathed in the true incense of precepts and samadhi — like one perfumed by incense whose body bears the fragrance — under the protection of the majestic light of fragrance she escaped calamity and dissolved the hindrances of misfortune. This is a shining example for later learners, and so it is specially cited in the hymn.

The story of Yasodhara: Before Shakyamuni Buddha left home he was Prince Siddhartha, and Yasodhara was his wife. Six years after the prince left home, Yasodhara gave birth to a son, Rahula. Everyone said, “How can this be? The prince has been away from home for six years, and yet Yasodhara has given birth to a child! Surely she has not kept to her virtue!” At that time the customs of India were extremely harsh; a woman had to be chaste, and if she were not, she would be burned alive. So they dug a pit, set the wood within it alight, and were about to burn Yasodhara and Rahula alive. Then Yasodhara said, “If I am chaste, then neither I nor my child will be burned, and a lotus flower will spring forth to protect us.” Having spoken, she gathered her mind in one place and leapt in. In truth a lotus flower appeared from the fire, catching and holding up the mother and child. Thus Yasodhara, because she strictly held the precepts and samadhi, “escaped calamity and dissolved the hindrances of misfortune.” Why could Yasodhara escape the calamity by saying she would? Because in both her past lives and this life she held the precepts and samadhi with utmost strictness.

blocks.text: The Sea of Awakening Arose From the Void

inline.s: The sea of awakening arose from the void; the waves of karma in the Saha world flow on;
If a person would reach the other shore, the Land of Bliss holds the boat of return.

The sea of awakening arises depending on the void, while in the Saha world (this shore) the waves of karma flow every which way; for you to ascend to the other shore of nirvana, the Land of Ultimate Bliss holds the boat for returning home (becoming a Buddha).

This verse is the guiding principle of the whole piece: for the beings of the unseen (the dead) and the seen (the living) in the Saha world, to escape transmigration and realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the most excellent path is to recite the Buddha’s name and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
“The sea of awakening arose from the void:”
The sea of awakening arises depending on the void,
and the myriad things are suddenly manifest,

and only then do the two shores (this shore of birth and death and the other shore of nirvana) begin to be divided. Between the shore of birth and death and the other shore of nirvana the sea of awakening lies across. The “sea of awakening” is a metaphor: the journey of awakening is like crossing a great sea — perilous and long. The ancients said:
“Borrow a raft in the deluded ford; cast a boat in the sea of awakening.”
[The sea of awakening arises depending on the void] This is the first deluded stirring of a single thought, whereby one enters the dream of ignorance (see further the
Dream of Ignorance
essay
), and falsely manifests objects. The Surangama Sutra says:
“In delusion there is empty space; depending on space the worlds are established; when thought settles it becomes lands; consciousness is the living beings.”
“The waves of karma in the Saha world flow on:”
This Saha world in which we dwell (this shore of birth and death),
the karma created by living beings rolls like a surging torrent, fierce and overwhelming, overflowing into calamity.
“If a person would reach the other shore:”
You should ascend to the other shore of nirvana (become a Buddha).
[Ruo ren (if a person)] You, you all; the meaning is the same as “ruo bei.” Here “ruo” means you, you all.
“The Land of Bliss holds the boat of return:”

The Land of Ultimate Bliss holds a jeweled boat that goes straight to the other shore of nirvana. Living beings reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss attain the stage of non-retrogression (avivartika) and realize Buddhahood in a single lifetime. Hence it is said, “The Land of Bliss holds the boat of return.” This is a metaphor: once one reaches the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there is a jeweled boat that, riding the wind and cleaving the waves, crosses the sea of awakening and goes straight to the other shore of nirvana, without needing to swim across alone (swimming alone across the sea is a metaphor for the common path relying wholly on one’s own power to remove afflictions and sever ignorance — a course of incomparable peril and difficulty). Hence Universal Worthy’s Ten Great Vows lead back to the Land of Bliss.

[The boat of return] The boat for returning home. Living beings are originally Buddha; now, dwelling deludedly in the Saha world, they are wandering in a foreign land, and ascending to the other shore of nirvana (becoming a Buddha) is returning home. [Living beings are originally Buddha] The Perfect Awakening Sutra says:
“Then you know that living beings are originally Buddha; birth, death, and nirvana are like a dream of last night.”

[Birth, death, and nirvana like a dream of last night] Birth, death, and nirvana are all matters in the dream of ignorance. Now that the dream of ignorance has ended, looking back at past affairs is like the dream of last night. (See further the
Detailed Explanation of the Perfect Awakening Sutra

[Universal Worthy’s Ten Great Vows lead back to the Land of Bliss] Universal Worthy Bodhisattva, by means of the Ten Great Vows, leads back to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, encouraging Sudhana the youth and the forty-one stages of Dharma-body great beings of the Hua-yang sea-host to direct their merit toward rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, in order to perfect the fruit of Buddhahood. On this, Master Yinguang gave this instruction:

“In the Hua-yang sea there are limitless Pure Lands, yet one must direct one’s merit toward rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. From this it may be known that rebirth in the Land of Bliss is the mysterious gate of leaving suffering
(an extremely wondrous method)
, and the shortcut to Buddhahood.”

(From “Resolving Doubts on the Pure Land”) [The Hua-yang sea] Hua-yang is an abbreviation for the lotus-store world, the land of Vairocana Buddha, the true body of Shakyamuni Tathagata. Because within the lotus are concealed worlds as numerous as dust-motes, it is called the Hua-yang sea. [An extremely wondrous method] The wonder and subtlety of the Buddha-recitation method can be known only by Buddha and Buddhas.

blocks.text: Discourse One: Reverently Hearing the Wondrous Dharma

inline.s: The King of Dharma benefits beings, with compassion and wisdom vast and deep,
Pervading the ten directions, among the unseen and the seen there is no separation.

Amitabha Buddha saves living beings; his compassionate mind and wondrous wisdom are deep, vast, and endless, reaching to the ten directions; in the unseen world and the seen world there is no obstruction.

[The King of Dharma] The Buddha, sovereign and free over the Dharma, is called the King of Dharma. Here it refers to Amitabha Buddha. [Wu (the beings)] The multitude of beings; for example, “the expectations of the multitude.” Here “wu” means all living beings. [Mi (
mǐ
)] without, none.
Now, receiving the patron
so-and-so
, reverently on behalf of
so-and-so
, at the occasion of
so-and-so

, I specially invite this mountain monk to ascend the seat, and in reliance upon the teaching of the Buddha to perform the Three Sessions of Mind-Recollection rite. This departed spirit, meeting such a splendid karmic occasion, should of himself be solemn in bearing and demeanor, and come before the seat, reverently hearkening to the wondrous Dharma, with single mind accepting the deliverance.
Today, receiving the kindness of the patron
so-and-so
, reverently on behalf of
so-and-so
, at the very occasion of
so-and-so

, I specially invite this mountain monk (a humble term) to ascend the Dharma seat and, according to the Buddha’s teachings, to perform the Three Sessions of Mind-Recollection rite. You departed spirits, encountering such an excellent karmic occasion, should be solemn in dress and bearing, come beneath the seat, reverently listen to the wondrous Dharma, and with single mind and utmost sincerity accept the deliverance.
[The patron] The donor who gives vegetarian food offerings. [The mountain monk] A monk of the wild mountains (a humble self-reference).

blocks.text: Discourse Two: Burning Incense as Offering

inline.s: This single petal of incense: its root coils beyond the aeon, its branches spread through the world of dust; it was not brought forth by heaven and earth — how could it belong to the creative work of yin and yang?

This single petal of incense (the true incense): its root coils back to before the beginningless aeon, its branches and leaves spread and flourish in the human world; it was not brought forth by heaven and earth, nor created and evolved by yin and yang.

[Incense] Here incense signifies the true incense of precepts and samadhi, following the above “Hymn of Praise on the True Incense of Precepts and Samadhi.” [A petal of incense] Because the form of incense resembles a melon petal, it is called a petal of incense. The Grove of Matters in Patriarchal Halls says:
“Venerable masters of ancient and modern times, when holding up incense, mostly say ‘a petal.’”
[World of dust] The human world.

Burned in the censer, it is offered with single-minded devotion. To the ever-abiding Three Jewels, to the myriad spirits of the sea of lands, to the guide of the Land of Bliss Amitabha Buddha, to Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, to the pure sea-host — all rely upon this true incense, and to all alike we make offering.

The incense (true incense) burns in the censer of the mind, offered sincerely with single devotion. The ever-abiding (the monastery), the Three Jewels (the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, the Sangha-jewel), all living beings of the ten directions, the guide of the Land of Bliss Amitabha Buddha, Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, and the pure sea-host of bodhisattvas — all rely upon this true incense, and to all alike we make offering.
sea of lands
The full term is “the great sea of lands,” referring to the worlds of the ten directions.
[The myriad spirits] All sentient living beings.

blocks.text: Discourse One: Merely Settling One’s Own Mind

inline.s: Why is the world called Ultimate Bliss? Because none of the host of sufferings can invade it;
If the person of the Way would seek the road home, he has but to settle his own mind amid the dusts.

Why is the world called Ultimate Bliss? Because none of the host of sufferings can invade it; if the practitioner would seek the road home, this road is: but to settle his own mind amid the six dusts (extinguish the deluded mind).
[Why is the world called Ultimate Bliss? Because none of the host of sufferings can invade it] In the Buddha Speaks the Amitabha Sutra, the Buddha says:
“Why is that land called Ultimate Bliss? Because the beings of that land have none of the host of sufferings but receive only manifold bliss; therefore it is called Ultimate Bliss.”

[The six dusts] Form-dust, sound-dust, fragrance-dust, taste-dust, touch-dust, and dharma-dust. “Dust” has the sense of defilement, meaning it can defile the pure minds of people so that the true nature cannot be manifested. They are also called the six objects, that is, the objects upon which the six sense-roots (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind) rely.
This verse is the prelude; the discourse that follows explains how to settle one’s own mind.
Mind after mind is Buddha; the ti-wei and su-lao all arise from milk; Buddha after Buddha is only mind; hairpins, bracelets, vases, and plates all come from gold.
“Mind after mind is Buddha; the ti-wei and su-lao all arise from milk:”
To transform the deluded mind into the true mind is to be Buddha. Know that the bodhisattvas of the various stages, and even the Buddhas, all come from ordinary people!
[Mind after mind is Buddha] To transform the deluded
mind
(the first word “mind”) into the true
mind

(the second word “mind”) is to be Buddha. [The ti-wei and su-lao all arise from milk] This is a metaphor: the Buddha and living beings are different states of the self-nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When the self-nature is deluded, that is a living being; when the self-nature is awakened, that is a Buddha.”

[The ti-wei and su-lao all arise from milk] When milk is refined one obtains butter (lao); when butter is refined one obtains su; and when su is refined one obtains ti-wei. The Indians not only regard ti-wei as “the first supreme flavor in the world,” but also hold it to have extremely high medicinal value. Here milk, butter, su, and ti-wei are used to metaphorically express the different stages of practice: milk represents ordinary people, butter and su represent the bodhisattvas of the various stages, and ti-wei represents the Buddha.
“Buddha after Buddha is only mind; hairpins, bracelets, vases, and plates all come from gold:”

For living beings to become Buddha, they too have only to transform the deluded mind into the true mind, because ordinary people, the bodhisattvas of the various stages, and even the Buddhas are identical in nature, differing only through the delusion or awakening of the self-nature.
[Buddha after Buddha is only mind] The principle-identity
Buddha
(the first word “Buddha,” which is a living being), to become the ultimate-identity
Buddha

(the second word “Buddha,” the Buddha of fully perfected fruit), likewise has only to transform the deluded mind into the true mind. [Hairpins, bracelets, vases, and plates all come from gold] The gold vessels — hairpins, bracelets (chuan, bangles), vases, and plates — are all likewise made of gold; their nature is the same, only their forms differ. A metaphor: living beings and the Buddha are identical in nature; the former is deluded, the latter awakened. [The principle-identity Buddha and the ultimate-identity Buddha] The first and the last of the two stages among the six identities of Buddha.
[The six identities of Buddha] Established by Great Master Zhizhe of the Tiantai school, to show the stages by which an ordinary person cultivates and realizes the fruit of Buddhahood:

First, the principle-identity Buddha. All living beings, though they transmigrate through the six realms and dwell daily amid the dust-and-toil of afflictions, turning their backs upon the awakened substance, nevertheless fully possess the merit of Buddha-nature; hence they are called “the principle-identity Buddha.”
The Buddha Speaks the Maha Parinirvana Sutra says:
“Know that liberation is itself the Tathagata. That which is the Tathagata is the Tathagata-nature, which is present within the bodies of all living beings.”

Second, the name-identity Buddha. Whether from a good teacher or from the scriptures, having heard of the inherent, unborn, and undying Buddha-nature, and through the name having comprehended and understood that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas and that all living beings can become Buddhas — nodding in assent, with a sudden opening of understanding — one is called “the name-identity Buddha.”

Third, the contemplation-practice identity Buddha. This is the position of the five grades, the outer-ordinary stage of the Perfect teaching. Not only comprehending the name, but further, in accordance with the teaching, cultivating contemplation, knowing that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; the contemplation of the mind is clear, the wisdom of principle responds; hence one is called “the contemplation-practice identity Buddha.”

Fourth, the semblance-identity Buddha. This is the stage of the ten faiths, the inner-ordinary position of the Perfect teaching: the first faith severs the delusion of views, the seventh faith severs the delusion of thought, and the eighth, ninth, and tenth faiths sever the delusion of dust-and-sand. The practitioner at this stage, in contemplation and practice, the more he contemplates the clearer, the more he stills the more serene; though he has not truly awakened or truly realized, yet in the principle he resembles it, as if truly realized; hence he is called “the semblance-identity Buddha.”

Fifth, the partial-realization identity Buddha. This is at the last thought of the ten faiths: breaking one portion of ignorance and realizing one portion of the three virtues, one enters the first dwelling and realizes the Dharma body; from then on one becomes a Dharma-body great being. From the first dwelling onward, each stage breaks one portion of ignorance and realizes one portion of the three virtues, up to the stage of equal enlightenment, passing through forty-one stages altogether and breaking forty-one portions; hence one is called “the partial-realization identity Buddha.”

Sixth, the ultimate-identity Buddha. This is when, from equal enlightenment, one breaks the final portion of ignorance; then delusion is exhausted and truth is pure, and one thoroughly realizes the inherent thusness Buddha-nature of one’s own body, entering the stage of wondrous enlightenment and becoming a Buddha; hence one is called “the ultimate-identity Buddha.”
A journey of a hundred thousand kotis, yet east and west are not separated; within the twelve hours, the ordinary and the holy share the same road.

Although the Saha world and the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss are separated by a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands, in fact they are not divided; throughout the twenty-four hours, Amitabha Buddha is with me.
This means: once awakened, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is right before one’s eyes, and Amitabha Buddha is with me day and night.
[East and west]
The Saha world (east) and the Land of Ultimate Bliss (west).
[The twelve hours]
The twelve double-hours. In antiquity a full day and night was divided into twelve double-hours. Here “twelve hours” means the whole day and night.
[The ordinary and the holy]“
The ordinary” refers to the living beings of the Saha world; “the holy” refers to Amitabha Buddha.

Bowing the head, palms joined, before the white-jade hair, bright as stars and radiant as the sun; singing hymns of praise to the purple-golden countenance, like a peal of thunder and a crash of lightning.

Bowing the head and joining palms in worship of Amitabha Buddha, one’s own mind is clear and bright, like the brilliance of stars, the splendor of the sun; singing hymns in praise of Amitabha Buddha, the sound is like a peal of thunder, a crash of lightning, echoing through the universe.
[The white-jade hair, the purple-golden countenance]
Amitabha Buddha has a purple-golden body, with a white-jade hair between the brows; therefore this represents Amitabha Buddha.
[Ting] A thunderbolt.
The cool moon! It is contained in all waters; the cloud of merit! There is no mountain it does not crown.

[The cool moon, contained in all waters] The bright moon hangs in the sky, its reflection appearing in a thousand rivers and ten thousand waters. A metaphor for Amitabha Buddha dwelling in the heart of every living being: if one single-mindedly recites the Buddha’s name, there is a meeting of mind and the Way. [The cloud of merit, no mountain it does not crown] A metaphor for Amitabha’s merit being present everywhere, benefiting every living being.

The fragrant elephant fords the river; with one raising of the great name one transcends the two deaths; the Kalavinka emerges from its shell; a thousand utterances of the lovely name surpass all other sounds.

[The fragrant elephant fords the river] A fragrant elephant (a great elephant) fording a river cuts its flow and reaches the bottom. A metaphor: Buddha-recitation severs birth and death. [With one raising of the great name one transcends the two deaths] Chanting Amitabha’s name severs the two deaths (the death of delimited life and the birth-and-death of transformation). [The death of delimited life] Living beings in the three realms and six paths, because their life spans and bodies are delimited by their good and evil karma, have a birth-and-death called “the death of delimited life.” One who has ended the death of delimited life escapes transmigration and leaves the three realms. [The birth-and-death of transformation] The sages of the three vehicles, having severed the delusions of views and thought and ended the death of delimited life, in the course of practice gradually dissolve delusions and increase realization; this shifting from delusion to awakening differs in each stage, and the transition from one stage to the next is like a passage through death; hence it is called “the birth-and-death of transformation.” One who has ended the birth-and-death of transformation perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. [Kalavinka] An abbreviation of the Kalavinka bird, whose song is supremely beautiful. The Surangama Sutra says:
“The immortal song of the Kalavinka pervades the worlds of the ten directions.”

[The Kalavinka emerges from its shell] A metaphor: a living being becoming a Buddha-recitater is like the Kalavinka emerging from its shell. [A thousand utterances of the lovely name surpass all other sounds] The sound of Buddha-recitation surpasses all other sounds, meaning the Buddha-recitation method is more excellent than all other methods.
The lowly feelings can only suppose
cǔn
, to infer)
what is hard to conceive, yet with a single thought turning back the light it is easy to go. In the ultimate sense it is not outside the mind; it is clearly right before the eyes.

Ordinary people are utterly unable to fathom the wonder and subtlety of the Pure Land method with their emotive consciousness; but if they but turn their thought back to the sacred name of Amitabha Buddha, they will very easily be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. For in the ultimate sense the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not outside the mind; it is clearly right before one’s eyes.
If this is truly so, then this present assembly, recollecting Amitabha in the three sessions of Buddhist rite, no longer needs to be concerned with realization and practice.

If they can indeed hear the above discourse, and in a single thought turn back the light and settle their own minds (extinguish the deluded mind), then today’s three sessions of Mind-Recollection rite no longer need to concern themselves with how to cultivate and how to realize.

[If this is truly so] Truly so. [Not concerned with realization and practice] If the departed spirit truly, in a single thought, turns back the light and settles its own mind, it is at once delivered and no longer needs cultivation and realization. Hence the following passage — “As for the phase ‘personally receiving the prediction,’ how is it proclaimed? The wind sings in the trees a thousand kinds of music,
the fragrance steeps each pool with four-colored lotus” — is the presiding master bestowing the prediction that the delivered departed spirit will be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[The wind sings in the trees a thousand kinds of music, the fragrance steeps each pool with four-colored lotus]
This depicts the scenery of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[The four-colored lotus] The Buddha Speaks the Amitabha Sutra says:

“In the ponds the lotus flowers are as large as cartwheels; blue light for the blue, yellow light for the yellow, red light for the red, white light for the white, subtly wondrous, fragrant, and pure.”
As for the phrase “personally receiving the prediction” — how is it proclaimed?
The wind sings in the trees a thousand kinds of music; the fragrance steeps each pool with four-colored lotus.

[As for the phrase “personally receiving the prediction” — how is it proclaimed?] How is the phrase “personally receiving the prediction” proclaimed? [Prediction] The sense of recording a name: the Buddha, for a living being who has aroused the great mind, records in advance his name — after so many aeons, in such a place and such a land, becoming such a Buddha. Here the prediction is rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Personally receiving the prediction] The Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing, in his Certain Guidelines on the West, gave this instruction concerning his own past “personally receiving the prediction”:
“Long ago, in the time of Emperor Ming of the Jin, I received the body of a poor boy. Because of poverty I made the great vow, saying: ‘Because I
(owing to)
past karma
(the karmic offenses of former lives)

, I receive this bitter retribution. If today I do not see Amitabha Buddha and am not born in the Land of Bliss, and do not perfect all merit, then even if I lose my life I shall never retreat or rest.’ Having made this vow, for seven days and seven nights I single-mindedly and earnestly recollected, and at once my mind opened and I saw Amitabha Buddha’s excellent marks and radiant light pervading the worlds of the ten directions. Before the Buddha I personally received the prediction, and afterward at age seventy-five I sat upright and passed away, and was in fact born in the Land of Bliss.

You should be single-minded in this method, firmly cultivating it; you will certainly not be mistaken. If your resolve is firm, you need not wait for the next life to be born; even in the present you shall see the Buddha, just as I did in former years.”
(See further the
Certain Guidelines on the West (Annotated)

) [The wind sings in the trees a thousand kinds of music; the fragrance steeps each pool with four-colored lotus] These two lines depict the scenery of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss: the wind blows the rows of trees and produces every kind of wondrous sound, and the four-colored (blue, yellow, red, white) lotus flowers perfume the seven-jeweled ponds everywhere. This is the prediction: one is certain to be born in the Land of Bliss.

blocks.text: Discourse Two: Realizing the Non-arising Dharma

inline.s: All the various sufferings arise entirely from greed and desire; do you not know from what greed and desire arise?
Because one forgets the self-nature Amitabha Buddha; stray thoughts running every which way are forever the devil.
All

the various sufferings arise entirely from greed and desire; and from what then do greed and desire arise? The answer lies in the next two lines: “Because one forgets the self-nature Amitabha Buddha; stray thoughts running every which way are forever the devil.”

[The self-nature Amitabha Buddha] The self-nature of living beings inherently possesses the Tathagata’s wisdom, virtue, and power, not two, not different from Amitabha Buddha; hence it is called the self-nature Amitabha Buddha. It is only that living beings are deluded and cannot realize it.
The Diamond Sutra says:
“If you see that all forms are non-forms, then you see the Tathagata.”
(See further the
Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
) The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Know your own mind; see your own nature.”
These are the essential methods for not forgetting the self-nature Amitabha Buddha. (See further the
Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Because one forgets the self-nature Amitabha Buddha; stray thoughts running every which way are forever the devil

Because one forgets that the self-nature is the true self, and takes this body and mind as “I” (entering the dream of transmigration), one gives rise to feelings of love and aversion, and deluded thoughts (stray thoughts) run wild. Thus greed and desire arise along with feelings and thoughts (one is possessed by the devil), and driven by greed one creates every kind of karma; through karma one receives retribution, drawing upon oneself all the various sufferings, and birth and death transmigrate without end.
The Perfect Awakening Sutra says:
“All living beings, from the beginningless past, are all manner of inversion, like a lost man who mistakes all four directions
(just as a lost traveler confuses east, south, west, and north)
, falsely taking the four elements as the form of self and the shadows of the six dusts as the marks of the mind. ... Because of this false existence they revolve in birth and death.”
(See further the
Detailed Explanation of the Perfect Awakening Sutra
[Stray thoughts] Thoughts that are not right thought.

[The four elements] All material things in the world are composed of the four elements — earth, water, fire, and wind — hence the term “great”: the great earth, great water, great fire, great wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water wetness, fire warmth, wind motion. Here the four elements refer to the human body.

[The shadows of the six dusts] The many thoughts produced when the six sense-roots meet the six dusts; and because these thoughts are all false and unreal, they are called “the shadows of the six dusts” — the phantom reflections of meeting the six dusts.
The core of this chapter is the realization of the non-arising Dharma.
[Realizing the non-arising Dharma] Realizing the non-arising Dharma (the real marks of all dharmas). On the real marks of all dharmas, see further the
Real Marks of All Dharmas
essay. [The non-arising Dharma] All dharmas are phantoms; originally they never arose, hence they never cease. The Diamond Sutra says:
“All forms are false and delusive.”
The Vimalakirti Sutra,
Chapter Nine on Entering the Non-dual Dharma-gate, says:
“Dharmas originally are unborn; now they are also unceasing.”
The teaching says: non-arising yet arising, and the Dharma-nature is bright and still; arising yet non-arising, and the fruits of karma are manifestly present.
The teachings often say: "Arising yet non-arising, the dharma-nature is limpid and still (clear and luminous); non-arising yet arising, karmic fruits appear vividly real (as though truly present)."
[Vividly real] As though it were true.
These words mean: all things and phenomena are illusions, matters within the dream of ignorance. The Diamond Sutra says:
"All that has marks is false and delusive."

Though all things and phenomena arise, in reality no such thing occurs (arising yet non-arising); for the noble ones who have realized the dharma of non-arising, their dharma-nature is clear and limpid, unstained and undefiled (the dharma-nature is limpid and still). Seen from the side of phenomena, though there is non-arising, illusory appearances still occur (non-arising yet arising); sentient beings who have not realized the dharma of non-arising are turned about by these illusions, and the karma they create and the fruits they receive all appear vividly real (karmic fruits appear vividly real).

[Within the teachings] "Within the teachings" means "inside the teaching," also called "under the teaching." The Chan school, which transmits the mind with the mind and sets up no doctrine of written words, calls itself "outside the teachings"; all other schools, which have the Buddha's spoken teachings and written words to follow, are called "inside the teachings." The Chan school calls itself the Chan gate, and refers to all others as "within the teachings" or "under the teachings." Master Zhongfeng was a Chan master, and so he spoke in this way. [Dharma-nature] The intrinsic nature of all dharmas. This intrinsic nature of all dharmas is called "Buddha-nature" in the case of sentient beings, and "dharma-nature" in the case of insentient things.
What is called arising is simply the trace of birth and death as seen by sentient beings; what is called non-arising is simply the ground of quiescent extinction as realized by the Buddhas.

This passage explains the "arising" and "non-arising" spoken of above: what is called arising is the illusory trace of dharmas suddenly born and suddenly extinguished as seen by sentient beings; what is called non-arising is the essential true aspect of dharmas, neither arising nor ceasing, as seen by the Buddhas (the true aspect of all dharmas). The text later says:
"Therefore the Buddhas, amid the vividly real arising and ceasing, see only non-arising; sentient beings, amid the limpid and still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing."
This limpid and still dharma-nature is spiritually luminous yet profoundly quiescent, mysterious and wondrous, true and constant; none lack it, every one possesses it innately.

What is called the limpid and still dharma-nature is the Buddha-nature innately possessed by every sentient being: spiritually luminous yet profoundly quiescent, mysterious and wondrous, true and constant.

[Spiritually luminous yet profoundly quiescent, mysterious and wondrous, true and constant] This describes the Buddha-nature innately possessed by every sentient being (that is, the dharma-nature of sentient beings).

"Spiritual" means not the insensibility of wood and stone; "luminous" means bright and clear; "profoundly quiescent" means clear and limpid, holding not a single thing; "mysterious and wondrous" means deep, subtle, and capable of all things; "true and constant" means truly existing, without beginning or end.
Only because of the first non-awakening, a mind suddenly stirred, and one took the false as real, lost oneself, and chased after things.
Only because of the first non-awakening, a mind suddenly stirred, and one took illusions as real, lost one's own nature, and chased after outer things.

[The first non-awakening, a mind suddenly stirred] This is beginningless ignorance, also called fundamental ignorance. [Things] Everything outside the body is called a thing. [One's own nature] The primordial state of the self-nature. See
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
Thereby entangled in the net of karma, they wander through the five realms. Forever rising and sinking with birth and death, from ancient times to the present without a moment's pause.

And so they create karma and receive its retribution, entangled in the net of karma, wandering through the heavens, the human realm, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, and the hells, ceaselessly rising (rebirth in a good realm) and sinking (rebirth in an evil realm) with birth and death, from ancient times to the present without ever resting.

[Five realms] Also called the five destinations. The five realms are the heavens, humans, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. If six realms are spoken of, the asuras are added. They are not mentioned here because the asuras are included among the heavens, humans, animals, and hungry ghosts. (A Dictionary of the Three Stores)

You should know: arising arises from conditions, yet the dharma-nature does not arise together with conditions; ceasing ceases with conditions, yet the dharma-nature does not cease together with conditions. Therefore it is said: the dharma-nature is limpid and still. This is what is meant by arising yet non-arising.

You should know: arising arises because conditions (causes and conditions) come together, yet the dharma-nature does not arise because conditions come together; ceasing ceases because conditions disperse, yet the dharma-nature does not cease because conditions disperse. Therefore it is said: the dharma-nature is limpid and still, unchanging. This is what is meant by arising yet truly non-arising.

As for non-arising yet arising: sentient beings' delusion enters the mind, karma accumulates into fruit, and they undergo transmigration in vain. Deludedly perceiving arising and ceasing, upon the essence of the dharma-nature it is like a mirror showing images, like a pearl taking on colors.

Though there is non-arising, illusory appearances still occur (non-arising yet arising), and sentient beings' delusion (taking these illusions as real) enters the mind (is deeply rooted in the mind); thus karma accumulates into fruit, and they undergo transmigration in vain. Perceiving arising and ceasing deludedly in this way, upon the essence of their Buddha-nature it is like a bright mirror showing images, like a precious pearl reflecting all manner of colors.

You should know that the mirror's light is originally pure, and the pearl's essence leaves no trace; thing and mirror illumine each other, yet neither goes against color or image. The coming and going of those colors and images is just like the vivid reality of karmic fruit.

You should know that the mirror's light is originally pure and holds nothing, and the pearl's essence leaves no trace either; thing and mirror manifest each other, the pearl going not against color, the mirror going not against image. The coming and going of those colors and images is like karmic fruit that seems to be real (vividly real).
Therefore the Buddhas, amid the vividly real arising and ceasing, see only non-arising; sentient beings, amid the limpid and still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing.
Therefore, the Buddhas, amid vivid arising and ceasing, see only non-arising; while sentient beings, amid limpid and still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing.
Only because of the difference between delusion and awakening does direct perception differ. In truth, arising has no self-nature, and non-arising has no self-nature either.
Only because sentient beings and Buddhas differ in delusion and awakening does their direct perception differ. In reality, arising has no self-nature, and non-arising has no self-nature either.

[Direct perception] The direct reflection of things by the sense organs. [Self-nature] The term "self-nature" has two meanings in Buddhist learning: first, the wondrous, luminous spiritual capacity of all virtues, for example the self-nature of sentient beings (see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha

); second, it means a substantial entity, so "no self-nature" means having no substantial entity, being an illusion. "Arising has no self-nature, and non-arising has no self-nature either" means that both arising and non-arising are illusions, matters within the dream of ignorance. No self-nature is also called no-nature. The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says:
"All dharmas are without self-nature."
The Lotus Sutra says:
"One knows that all dharmas are forever without nature."
The Surangama Sutra says:
"All illusions become natureless."

Awakened, then arising and ceasing are all non-arising; deluded, then non-arising is all arising and ceasing. Therefore apart from this there is nothing else; it is one substance under different names.

Awakened, then the myriad phenomena of arising and ceasing are all limpid and still non-arising; deluded, then the limpid and still non-arising is all the myriad phenomena of arising and ceasing. Therefore apart from this there is nothing else; arising and non-arising are simply different ways of seeing and speaking about one and the same substance.

[It is one substance under different names] This is like the example of "flowers in the sky" often given in the sutras and treatises: a person with an eye disease sees flowers in the sky, while a person without the eye disease sees no flowers in the sky. When the former's eye disease is cured, he too will see that there were never any flowers in the sky. Flowers in the sky and no flowers in the sky are simply different ways of seeing and speaking about one and the same matter by a person whose eyes are abnormal and one whose eyes are normal. Another example: a person with floaters sees black specks dancing before his eyes, while a person with healthy eyes sees no black specks dancing before that person's eyes. Black specks dancing and no black specks dancing — this is one substance under different names.

If this is so, then Amitabha Buddha is my own mind, and my own mind is Amitabha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, and this very place is the Pure Land. Is this not simply because delusion and awakening differ of themselves? How can there be sage and ordinary being, this and that?

If one truly realizes that arising and ceasing are all non-arising, then Amitabha Buddha is my own mind, and my own mind is Amitabha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, and this very place is the Pure Land. Is it not simply that these differences arise from delusion and awakening being different? In reality, where is there a "that" sage and a "this" ordinary being?
Then one knows that the assembly now present, by means of the self-nature Amitabha, together with the tongue-roots of the great assembly, universally turn the root dharma wheel.

Having reached this point, one knows that the people now present are, by means of the self-nature Amitabha Buddha together with the Buddha-recitation of the great assembly's mouths, universally proclaiming the teaching of the One Vehicle.

[Turning the root dharma wheel] Proclaiming the teaching of the One Vehicle. It is one of the three dharma wheels. [Three dharma wheels] Also called the three turnings of the dharma wheel: first, the root dharma wheel, which refers to the Buddha's first attainment of the Way, when he taught the Avatamsaka Sutra to the bodhisattvas; it belongs to the One Vehicle teaching and is the root of all dharmas, and so is called the "root dharma wheel." Second, the branch-and-tip dharma wheel: because sentient beings found the One Vehicle teaching hard to understand, the Buddha then taught the Agama, Prajna, Vaipulya, and other sutras; these sutras are branch and tip in relation to the root, and so are called the "branch-and-tip dharma wheel." Third, the dharma wheel of gathering the branches back to the root: this refers to the Buddha's teaching of the Lotus Sutra, which joins the Three Vehicles into the One Buddha Vehicle, that is, gathering the branches back to the root, and so is called the "dharma wheel of gathering the branches back to the root." [One Vehicle] Also called the "One Buddha Vehicle," the only teaching that can lead people to Buddhahood.
Do all you virtuous ones fully understand?
Have all you virtuous ones fully and clearly understood?
[Virtuous one] A respectful address to others.
Arising and ceasing are non-arising; is there arising or not? Would the Land of Bliss ever bar anyone's way?
Who would have guessed that amid ten thousand fathoms of red dust, water lilies open as the moon shines bright?

Arising and ceasing are non-arising; is there arising or not? Would the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (the Land of Bliss) ever forbid anyone to go? Who would have guessed that right here, amid ten thousand fathoms of red dust, lotus flowers bloom in pond after pond while a single bright moon shines clearly?

[Arising and ceasing are non-arising] That is, as said above, "awakened, then arising and ceasing are all non-arising." [Is there arising or not] This asks whether one will be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss or not. [Would the Land of Bliss ever bar anyone's way] That is: whether or not one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss depends entirely on oneself. Master Yinguang says:
"It is only that you do not return; return and you have it. Who would contend for the wind and moon of your native place?"

Here the native place is a metaphor for the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss: it is only natural that you should go home, so who would stand in your way? The question is whether you yourself go back or not. Therefore Master Zhongfeng says: would the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss ever forbid anyone to go? [Water lily (
hàn dàn

)] The lotus. [Who would have guessed that amid ten thousand fathoms of red dust, water lilies open as the moon shines bright] This means that this very place is the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (as said above:
"This very place is the Pure Land."

). [Red dust] The human world. The term "red dust" came into use in the Tang dynasty. Because the capital Chang'an lay in the northwest on loess soil, and in prosperous times Chang'an was always crowded with carriages and horses, the dust raised at sunset looked red to the people of Chang'an then, and so there arose the expression "red dust." Later the term was used to describe the mundane world and the human realm.

blocks.text: Instruction Three: One Thought Turns Against the Truth

inline.s: In every person's share, Amitabha is originally present; in every single mind, there is always the Pure Land. Understand, and you see the Buddha in everything; awaken, and every step is the West.

In every person's share, Amitabha Buddha is originally present; in every single mind, there is always the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Understanding (penetrating the dharma of non-arising), then one sees Amitabha Buddha in every matter (one's own nature is Amitabha Buddha); awakening (realizing the dharma of non-arising), then every step is the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (one's own mind is the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss).

This speaks of "the Amitabha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind only." Buddha-recitation by holding the name has two modes: practice in terms of phenomena and practice in terms of principle. Reciting Amitabha Buddha of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is practice in terms of phenomena; reciting the Amitabha of one's own nature is practice in terms of principle. (For practice in terms of principle, see
A Detailed Explanation of A Sketch of the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi

Practice in terms of principle must be undertaken on the basis of already having attained single-mindedness in practice in terms of phenomena, only then can one avoid the disaster of falling into emptiness. Master Yinguang says:

"Because of the Amitabha of one's own nature, one must recite the Amitabha of the West and seek rebirth there; by gradual progress one may then personally realize the Amitabha of one's own nature. If one clings only to the Amitabha of one's own nature and does not recite the Amitabha of the West, then even if one truly awakens
(sees the mind and sees the nature)
, one still cannot at once end birth and death."
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
in Answer to Layman Qu Tianxiang's Twenty-Seven Questions)

[One still cannot at once end birth and death] Ending birth and death by one's own power requires cutting off every affliction utterly. Therefore after seeing the mind and seeing the nature, one must still do the work of guarding and sustaining it in order to cut off every affliction utterly.
The pure-karma practice ground of the three sessions of mindfulness has been established as above; now the Buddha-work of the first session is complete.
From the foregoing, the pure-karma practice ground of the three sessions of mindfulness has been established; now the Buddha-work of the first session is brought to completion.
[As above] The foregoing, what has been stated above.
The outstanding merit as above is cast into Amitabha's great ocean of vows, dedicated specifically to the many spirits on the rebirth hall's tablets, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.

The outstanding merit as above is cast into Amitabha Buddha's great ocean of vows, dedicated specifically to the many spirits on the rebirth hall's tablets, seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

But we reflect that from beginningless time until this present life, one thought turned against the truth, and the six faculties chased after the false, creating karma with the afflictions, indulging the self in wrongdoing.

But we reflect that from beginningless time until this present life, because one thought turned against the truth, the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) chased after illusory appearances, and following emotions and desires they ceaselessly created karma, indulging themselves in doing evil.

In bodily karma there are killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; in faults of speech there are lying, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh speech; in evil of mind there is the constant arising of greed and anger, and the deep growth of deluded craving.

Bodily karma is killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; faults of speech are lying, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh speech; evil of mind is the constant arising of greed and anger, and the deep growth of deluded craving.
Through these three karmas, hooked and locked to false conditions, one is forever churning amid the toils of dust, and only blindly wastes the years.
Through these three karmas of body, speech, and mind, hooked and locked to false conditions, one is forever hurrying amid worldly affairs, and only blindly wastes the years.
[Gurgling (
gǔ gǔ
)] Describes the sound or appearance of flowing water.
If one wishes to leave it all behind, one can rely only on the power of repentance and sustained cultivation. Let
bǐ
the transgressions of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind be at once dissolved as one recollects; let the floating dust of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma be at once purified.

If one wishes to escape birth and death, one can rely only on the power of repentance and sustained cultivation. Let the faults and errors of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind be at once dissolved as one recollects; let the floating dust of affliction of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma be at once purified.

Moreover, seeking rebirth in the Land of Bliss depends entirely on making vows. We respectfully trouble the assembly of Dharma, with one voice and one accord, to reverently repent and make vows for the spirits with all their hearts.

Moreover, seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss depends entirely on making vows. We respectfully trouble the great assembly of the Dharma gathering, with one voice and one accord, to reverently repent and make vows for the spirits with all their hearts.

blocks.text: Instruction Four: Manifesting Freely with the Mind

inline.s: The repentance and vow-making above are now concluded.
From the foregoing, the repentance and vow-making are now concluded.

The many spirits on the rebirth hall's tablets should know: the teaching of the Pure Land relies upon Amitabha Buddha's forty-eight great, compassionate, profound and weighty vows, which gather in all sentient beings of the ten directions. All who possess faith attain rebirth.

You many spirits on the rebirth hall's tablets should know: the doctrine of the Pure Land practice is to rely upon the great compassion and the profound, weighty power of Amitabha Buddha's forty-eight vows, which gather in all sentient beings of the ten directions for rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. All who possess faith attain rebirth.
[All who possess faith attain rebirth] Please note that the text later says:
"Faith without practice does not amount to faith."
Faith means believing that the Western Pure Land exists, believing that Amitabha Buddha gathers in sentient beings, and believing that we sentient beings have a share in rebirth.
Faith means believing that the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss exists, believing that Amitabha Buddha gathers in sentient beings, and believing that we sentient beings have a share in rebirth.

Yet although it is said that Amitabha gathers in sentient beings for rebirth, one must believe that this is only manifestation freely following the mind, the intertwining of stimulus and response, and in the end is not obtained from outside.

Yet although it is said that Amitabha Buddha gathers in sentient beings for rebirth, one must believe that this is manifestation freely following the mind, the intertwining of stimulus and response, and in the end is not obtained from outside.

[Only manifestation freely following the mind] The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When the mind-water is clear and still (quiet and limpid), the Buddha-moon appears; when the mind-water is stirred and turbid (moving and murky), though the Buddha-moon still shines, its reflection does not appear.
[The intertwining of stimulus and response] The stimulus of sentient beings and the response of Amitabha Buddha meet and interpenetrate.

Amitabha Buddha's coming to guide (gather in) sentient beings is only manifestation freely following the mind; this is because of the intertwining of stimulus and response, and is not obtained from outside. Therefore only those with right mindfulness at the time of death can see the Buddha come, while others around them cannot see it. As for dying sentient beings who lack right mindfulness at death, because their own minds are turbid and disordered and they have no stimulus of right mindfulness (ten continuous thoughts), naturally Amitabha Buddha's coming to guide them will not manifest in their minds either, and so they do not see the Buddha come — it is not that Amitabha Buddha does not come to guide them. Therefore whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has right mindfulness at the time of death (ten continuous thoughts at death).
One who has faith in this way has true faith.
One who has faith in this way alone has true faith.

Faith without practice does not amount to faith. As for practice, the Surangama Sutra says: "Gather in all six faculties, and pure thoughts continue without interruption; without resort to expedient means, the mind opens of itself."

Faith without practice cannot bring faith to completion. As for practice, the Surangama Sutra says: "Gather in all six faculties, and pure thoughts continue without interruption; without resort to expedient means, the mind opens of itself."

The Amitabha Sutra says: If there be good men or good women who hear of Amitabha Buddha and hold fast to his name, whether for one day, for two days, or even for seven days, with single-mindedness and without confusion, then when such a person approaches the end of life, Amitabha Buddha together with all the sages will appear before him; and when that person's life ends, with a mind free of inversion, he will attain rebirth in Amitabha Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss.
One who practices in this way is said to practice the right practice.
One who thus holds fast to the name with single-mindedness and without confusion is said to practice the right practice.
Practice without vows does not amount to practice. As for vows, one should correspond vow for vow with Amitabha Buddha's forty-eight vows; this is the great vow.
Practice without vows cannot bring practice to completion. As for vows, one should correspond vow for vow with Amitabha Buddha's forty-eight vows; this alone is the great vow.
Faith, practice, and vow are like the three legs of a tripod: none may be missing.
Faith, practice, and vow are like the three legs of a tripod: none may be missing.

Now you spirits should know: the one thought before you is originally perfect and constant; faith, practice, and vow are originally what you yourself possess from the start. Such virtuous qualities of the nature are now merely the radiance of the original nature shining forth.

Now you spirits should know: the one thought before you is originally perfect and constant; faith, practice, and vow are originally what you yourself possess from the start. Such virtuous qualities of the nature are now merely the radiance of the original nature shining forth!

blocks.text: The Second Session of Dharma Work
Instruction One: Return and You Have It

inline.s: Were you to go and become a Buddha this very day, the Lord of the Land of Bliss would still call it late;
How much less could you abide such fine phrases and empty words? Be sure your transmigration would have no end.

Even if one were to go this very day to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and attain Buddhahood in one lifetime, Amitabha Buddha would still call it too late; how much worse to quibble over words and idly discuss theories now. Be assured that one's transmigration would then have no end.

[Were you to go and become a Buddha this very day, the Lord of the Land of Bliss would still call it late] Because all the past lives and deaths before this were wasted for nothing, and one could not attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Fine phrases] The words zhi, hu, ye, and zhe. All four are classical Chinese function words, ridiculing people who love to quibble over words. It also describes speech or writing that is half literary and half colloquial.

Originally: throughout the ten directions is the Land of Ultimate Bliss, its mountain light and water hues like emptiness meeting emptiness; the whole great earth is the pure and peaceful native place, where flowers smile and birds call like a mirror reflecting a mirror.

Originally, throughout the ten directions all is the Land of Ultimate Bliss, its mountain light and water hues like emptiness meeting emptiness; the whole great earth is the pure and peaceful native place, where flowers smile and birds call like a mirror reflecting a mirror.
[Originally] An introductory particle, meaning: originally this

. [Like emptiness meeting emptiness, like a mirror reflecting a mirror] This says that the mountain light and water hues of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and the smiling flowers and calling birds of the pure and peaceful native place, are likewise illusions, matters within the dream of ignorance. Then, since they are illusions, matters in a dream, why should one still strive to cultivate the Way in order to seek rebirth there? Because the Saha world is a nightmare and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is a sweet dream. In the nightmare of the Saha world, one is deluded again and again, suffering without end. But in the sweet dream of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one awakens again and again, until the dream of ignorance ends; moreover, there is none of the many sufferings, but only the receiving of all joys. On this point, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, gave this instruction: a Chan practitioner asked, "All dharmas are like a dream. The Saha world is certainly a dream, but the Land of Ultimate Bliss is a dream too. Since both are dreams, what benefit is there in cultivating within a dream?" I (Master Chewu) answered, "What you say is not right. Before the seventh bhumi, all is cultivation within a dream. As for the great dream of ignorance, even a bodhisattva of equal enlightenment has not fully awakened from it. Only the Buddha can be called thoroughly awakened. When the dreaming eye has not yet opened, the suffering and joy within the dream seem utterly real. Rather than undergo the extreme suffering of the Saha world within a dream, why not undergo the wondrous joy of the Land of Ultimate Bliss within a dream? Moreover, the dream of the Saha world is a passing from dream into further dream. Dreaming on and on, one grows ever more deluded and ever deeper. The dream of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is a passing from dream into awakening. Awakening on and on, one gradually awakens completely. Though the Saha world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss are both dreams, the nature of the two dreams is utterly different; how can they be lumped together?" (For the original text, see
A Treatise on Buddha-Recitation
: Cultivating the Way in a Dream
It is only that you do not return; return and you have it. Who would contend for the misty prospect of the five lakes?

It is entirely that you yourself are unwilling to go home (to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss); so long as you resolve to return you will certainly be able to return. Who would contend with you for the beautiful prospect of mist and cloud over the five lakes (meaning: who would block your way home just to contend for this beautiful prospect)?

[Return and you have it] So long as you resolve to return, you will certainly be able to return. For the requirement for rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is ten continuous thoughts at the time of death

, and this requirement can be met by every person through effort; unlike the ordinary-path practices, in which only a very few can end birth and death in this very life. Therefore it is said: in seeking rebirth through Buddha-recitation, "return and you have it."
[It is only that you do not return; return and you have it. Who would contend for the misty prospect of the five lakes] This is taken from the Tang poet Cui Tu's "Spring Night

The Water Flows On, the Flowers Fall, Both Heartless," using the native place as a metaphor for the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Five lakes] Lake Tai and the four lakes nearby. [Misty prospect] The beautiful scene wrapped in cloud and mist.
The golden arm hangs down always, day and night, and only the practitioner is fit to receive it; the white-rayed curl is undimmed through past and present, and only the one who vows can take it up.

The golden arm hangs down always, day and night (a metaphor for Amitabha Buddha's ceaseless guidance of sentient beings day and night), and only the cultivator is fit for it; the radiance of the white-rayed curl shines through past and present (a metaphor for Amitabha Buddha as the lighthouse guiding sentient beings in the bitter sea of birth and death from ancient times to now), and only the one who vows can take it up.
Therefore it is said: all dharmas are the light of the mind, all conditions are known only to the nature; originally there is no deluded or awakened person, only the need to finish it today.

Therefore it is said: all dharmas are the light of the mind, and all conditions are known only to one awakened to the self-nature; originally there is no deluded person or awakened person, and the essential thing is to finish with one's own mind today.
Now, with the assembly present here mindful in the second session of Buddha-work, how shall this one phrase be set forth?
Now, with the assembly present here mindful in the second session of Buddha-work, how shall it be summed up in a single phrase and proclaimed?
Above the glass-green pond hangs the bright moon; among the water lilies play the waterfowl.
This phrase is the prediction that those complete in faith, vow, and practice will "return and have it" (be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss).

blocks.text: Instruction Two: This Mind Is Buddha

inline.s: This mind is Buddha; with the mind recite the Buddha. Recite until the mind is empty and the Buddha too is forgotten.
Letting go and returning home, look around once more: the flowers open in red and white, in blue and yellow.

This mind is Buddha; with the mind recite the Buddha, reciting straight on until both grasper and grasped are gone. When life ends and one returns home, look around once more — ah! This is already the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[This mind is Buddha] This mind makes the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha. The Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says:

"All Buddhas, the Tathagatas, are the dharmakaya of the dharma-realm, entering into the minds and thoughts of all sentient beings. This mind is the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics. This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha."

[Recite until the mind is empty and the Buddha too is forgotten] This is the state in which Buddha-recitation reaches the point where both the grasper (the mind that recites) and the grasped (the Buddha-name recited) are gone. [Letting go and returning home, look around once more] "Letting go" means letting go of the dusty world (leaving the mundane world). "Returning home" means going home (attaining rebirth). "Look around once more" means examining one's surroundings afresh. [Flowers open in red and white, in blue and yellow] This is already the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. "Flowers open in red and white, in blue and yellow" — this
is the scenery of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, indicating that one has already arrived there.
The Buddha Speaks of Amitabha Sutra says:

"In the ponds are lotuses as large as chariot wheels, blue-colored with blue light, yellow-colored with yellow light, red-colored with red light, white-colored with white light, subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure."
Within the teachings it is said: "Mind and Buddha are likewise, Buddha and sentient beings are so too; mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction."
Within the teachings it is said: "Mind and Buddha are likewise, Buddha and sentient beings are so too; mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction."

[Mind and Buddha are likewise, Buddha and sentient beings are so too] The mind (self-nature) and the Buddha are the same (with no distinction between them), and Buddha and sentient beings are the same as well. This is spoken in terms of the ultimate essence (the dharmakaya). "Likewise" is a classical Chinese particle, often used at the beginning of a sentence; for example, "in the second month, after the full moon." "Are so too" means both are the same. [Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction] This says that the ultimate essence of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings is equal among all three, with no distinction. Here "mind" means the self-nature (not the consciousness-mind). And this ultimate essence is the dharmakaya. That is to say, the dharmakaya of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings is equal among all three, with no distinction. The Avatamsaka Sutra (sixty-fascicle version)
Chapter Sixteen, the Suyama Heaven Palace Bodhisattvas' Verses, says:
"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction."
This text says later:

"Therefore Buddha is sentient beings and sentient beings are Buddha; moreover, outside the mind there is no Buddha, nor are there sentient beings. Only because delusion and awakening differ is there a gap, and so sage and ordinary being are utterly different."
Now as for what is called the mind, the mind is of many kinds.
So-called mind is of many kinds.
There is the fleshly heart; it is that which, in the present body, is born of the father's and mother's blood and vital breath.
One is the fleshly heart; it is that which, in the present body, came from the blood and vital breath of one's parents.
There is the deliberating mind; it is that which, upon the circumstances of good and evil, favorable and adverse, produces every kind of discrimination.
One is the deliberating mind; it is that which, presently amid circumstances good and evil, favorable and adverse, gives rise to every sort of discrimination.

There is the numinous knowing mind; it mingles with a thousand differences yet is not confused, passes through the three times yet never shifts; bright and alone it shines, uplifted and beyond all company; in sages it is not increased, in ordinary beings it is not diminished. Dwelling in the stream of birth-and-death, the black dragon's pearl alone glows in the vast sea; resting upon the shore of nirvana, the cassia moon hangs solitary in the heavens.

One is the numinous knowing mind; amid a thousand differences it is not disturbed, passes through the three times (past, present, and future) without change, shining brightly it stands alone, aloof and independent. In sages it gains nothing; in ordinary beings it loses nothing. Dwelling in the stream of birth-and-death, it is like the pearl that glows alone in the vast sea; resting on the shore of nirvana, it is like the bright moon shining alone in the sky.
The black-dragon pearl: a treasure said to lie beneath the jaw of a black dragon, from the Zhuangzi
chapter “Lie Yukou”:
“A pearl worth a thousand pieces of gold must lie in a ninefold abyss, beneath the jaw of the black dragon.”
The cassia wheel: a name for the moon. After the Han and Jin dynasties the legend of a cassia tree in the moon became prevalent in Chinese myth, so the moon came to be called the cassia wheel.

Above we have spoken of three kinds of mind: the fleshly heart, the deliberating mind, and the numinous knowing mind. The fleshly heart is a bodily organ and has nothing to do with the mind of which the Dharma speaks. The deliberating mind and the numinous knowing mind, however, are the two states of the mind's delusion and its awakening.

The numinous knowing mind is empty and still, without a single thought, luminous and translucent, standing aloof and independent; this is the original state of the mind, and is therefore called the original mind — the state of the mind's awakening. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“If you do not recognize your original mind, studying the Dharma will avail you nothing. If you recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, you are called a great man, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.”

The original mind is undefiled, and is therefore also called the pure mind. The original mind is without knowledge and yet knows all things, and so it is called the numinous knowing mind. It should be noted that the “knowing” of the numinous knowing mind is a knowing of non-knowing (still and yet aware); in order to distinguish it from the grasping knowledge of seeing, hearing, and perception, it is called numinous knowing. The Surangama Sutra says:
“To set up knowledge within vision is the root of ignorance; when vision no longer abides in a seeing, that is nirvana, the undefiled and truly pure.”
Master Hanshan says in his Notes on the Lankavatara Sutra:
“When the mind is still and yet aware, apart from both the real and the false, it is called the self-awakened sage's wisdom.”

The deliberating mind is the mind that clings to the six sense-objects and arises from them; it is also called the consciousness mind, and is the state of the mind's delusion. Its traits are discrimination, calculation, delight and aversion, grasping and rejecting. The stirring of thoughts, seeing, hearing, and perception (in which the “knowing” is a discriminative knowing) — all these are the working of the consciousness mind.

Cultivation means awakening to the numinous knowing mind and guarding it at every moment without forgetting, first guarding and then letting be, until reaching the unconditioned. The Essentials of Mind-Cultivation says:
“One who awakens to this
(the numinous knowing mind)
and guards it sits in a single suchness and is liberated without movement; one who is deluded about it and turns from it goes among the six courses
(the six realms)
and revolves for long kalpas.”
(See
The Annotated Essentials of Mind-Cultivation

.) [Sitting in a single suchness] “To sit” means to abide firmly. “One” means non-duality; “such” means non-difference. Neither dual nor different is called a single suchness. “Sitting in a single suchness” means abiding firmly in suchness. In concrete practice, this means: think of neither good nor evil, do not grasp at marks, and remain still and unmoving. The Sixth Patriarch says:

“If you wish to know the essential of mind, simply think of neither good nor evil; then you will naturally enter the pure essence of mind, serene and ever still, its wondrous function as countless as the sands
(wondrous function without end, like the sands of the Ganges)
(See
The Annotated Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

.) [Guarding and letting be] After awakening (seeing one's nature), cultivation proceeds in two stages: first, guarding — protecting the mind from running after circumstances, so as to subdue affliction; second, letting be — allowing the mind to flow freely, no longer following circumstances, so as to cut off affliction. [Flowing freely] Allowing the mind to operate of itself.
All Buddhas, awakening to it, provisionally name it mind-only; sentient beings, deluded about it, turn it into false consciousness.

This mind, when the Buddhas awaken to it, is provisionally named mind-only (the numinous knowing mind); when sentient beings are deluded about it, it becomes false consciousness (the deliberating mind).

Therefore Buddha is exactly sentient beings, and sentient beings are exactly Buddha; and beyond mind there is no Buddha, nor any sentient being. Only because of the difference between delusion and awakening do ordinary beings and sages differ so greatly. How could one not know that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are without distinction in the three?

Therefore Buddha is exactly sentient beings, and sentient beings are exactly Buddha; and beyond the mind there is no Buddha, nor are there sentient beings. Only the difference between delusion and awakening separates the two, so that the ordinary person and the sage are far apart. Speaking of the ultimate, however, mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are without any difference.
Yongjia says: “In the dream there are clearly the six courses; after awakening, all is empty — the great thousand vanishes.”
Master Yongjia's Song of Realization says: “In the dream (the dream of ignorance) there are clearly the six courses (six realms); after awakening, all is empty — the great thousand vanishes.”
This is the state of having realized the unborn Dharma (see
The Annotation of the Song of Realization

Since this is so, then the sutra says: “Moving from this western direction past a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands, there is a world called Sukhavati; in it there is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is now teaching the Dharma.” All of this is nothing but the mind-only Pure Land and the original-nature Amitabha.

Since this is so, the Amitabha Sutra says: “Going from this western direction past a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands, there is a world called Sukhavati; in it is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is now expounding the Dharma.” None of it goes beyond the mind-only Pure Land and the self-nature Amitabha.
[The mind-only Pure Land, the original-nature Amitabha] This is the commonly known saying, “mind-only Pure Land, self-nature Amitabha.”

From this one may know: the multitudes of departed spirits now upon the hall of rebirth, in their life were attended by lotus bloom upon bloom, and in their passing rest beneath row upon row of jeweled trees; not for a moment were they apart from the land of the lotus, not for a single thought did they fail to rely upon the compassionate Father.

From this we know: the many departed spirits now upon the hall of rebirth, while alive were surrounded by lotus bloom after bloom, and after death rest beneath row upon row of jeweled trees; not for a moment have they left the world of bliss, not by a single thought do they fail to depend on Amitabha Buddha. (Only because sentient beings are deluded do they enter the dream of ignorance. If the dream of ignorance were once awakened, they would know they were already in the Pure Land.)
[Mo (
mò
)] To die.
