Reflecting thus, let me ask: apart from this mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, is there any other place to turn for converse?
Truly so, then let me ask: apart from this mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, is there still any other place to converse?
Within the great mirror not a speck of dust, within the emerald lotus lies the holy embryo,
Gazing afar beyond the golden-sand pools, precious light forever shines on the jade towers.

Within the great mirror (the numinous knowing mind) there is not a hair of dust; within the precious lotus there lies the holy embryo. Gazing afar beyond the golden-sand pool, precious light forever shines upon the jade towers.

[Within the great mirror not a speck of dust] This is a metaphor for the state in which the numinous knowing mind is present. [Jade lotus-root] In myth, the lotus-root eaten by the immortals. [Emerald lotus] The lotus in the seven-jeweled pool of the Western Pure Land. [Holy embryo] Before the beings who have been reborn in the Western Pure Land see the Buddha when the flower opens, they are called a holy embryo. [Golden-sand pool] The seven-jeweled pool whose bottom is spread with golden sand. [Gazing afar beyond the golden-sand pool] This describes the holy embryo looking outward from its own lotus.

blocks.text: The Third Instruction: A Water-Bubble upon the Great Sea

inline.s: Now I have heard: the empty gives forth a sounding response, the still has no form or shadow. Yet the valley's echo sounds of itself — it is not that it answers without a call; the Buddha's body does nothing of itself — it is not that it manifests without a knock.

It is often said: the empty yields a resonating reply, the still has no appearance of form or shadow. Yet the echo of a valley arises naturally; unless there is a call there will be no echoing sound. The Buddha's body does not deliberately act; only when sentient beings have a responsive faculty does Amitabha Buddha respond.
[Gai wen (I have heard)] “It is often said.” The word “gai” is a discourse-initial particle.
Now that the consecration of the second-period Buddha-recitation rite has been completed, the extraordinary merit above is cast into the great vow-sea of the Tathagata, from which virtue is born.
Having thus established the second-period recitation rite to its completion, this outstanding merit is plunged into the great vow-sea of the Tathagata, giving rise to virtue.

Especially for the many departed spirits upon the hall of rebirth, may it wash away the defilement of karma, increase their wholesome roots, release this karmic body, and lead them to rebirth in the Pure Land.

Especially for the many departed spirits upon the hall of rebirth, may it wash away the defilement of karma, increase their wholesome roots, relinquish this karmic body, and bring them rebirth in the Western Land of Bliss.
[Karmic body] The causal conditions of ripened retribution.
One should only reflect that since beginningless time, down to this present life, as a water-bubble
ōu
born upon the great sea, one rises and falls with the waves of consciousness; and as a cloud dotting the clear sky, one lets the wind of emotion create this self and that.

One should but reflect that since beginningless time, straight down to this present life, as a water-bubble born on the great sea one mounts and sinks with the waves of consciousness; as a cloud drifting across the vast heavens, one follows the wind of feeling and discriminates between self and other.

[Beginningless] All worlds, sentient beings, and all dharmas have no beginning. This life arises from the causes and conditions of a former life, and that former life too arises from the conditions of its own former life; tracing thus backward, the ultimate origin of sentient beings and of all dharmas can never be found. Hence it is called “beginningless.”
Thereupon: revolving through the various realms, transmigrating among the four modes of birth; the sea of karma is boundless, the mountain of guilt towers high.
Thereupon: revolving through the six realms, transmigrating among the four modes of birth; the sea of karma is trackless and vast, the mountain of guilt rises steep.
[Jiji (
jí jí

)] Describes a mountain rising steeply. [The six realms] Gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings. Since these six are the places to which all sentient beings go by the force of karma, they are also called the “six courses.” [The four modes of birth] Womb-birth, egg-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth. Womb-birth is a life that takes form within the mother's womb before being born, as with humans; egg-birth is a life that takes form within an eggshell before being born, as with birds; moisture-birth is a life that receives its form through moisture, as with insects; transformation-birth is a life that, with nothing to rely upon, is suddenly born by the power of karma alone, as are the gods, the hell-beings, and the humans at the beginning of an age.
If one does not rely upon open confession, how can it be dispelled?
Without relying on open confession, how can it be eliminated?
[Open confession] To disclose and declare the offenses one has committed without concealing anything. The Four Teachings Manual says:
“Confess everything freely, and conceal nothing further.”
Having repented of the past, make vows for what is to come. Once more, let the Dharma assembly with wholehearted minds repent and make vows.
Repent of the past, and vow for the future. Once more let the great assembly of the Dharma gathering, with single-hearted sincerity, repent and vow.
[Chanmo] Repentance.

blocks.text: The Fourth Instruction: Faith Is as the Eye

inline.s: To possess faith is as a man possessing eyes; the vow is the light of sun, moon, and lamp. Only by the light's illumination can one see clearly, and only then can the practitioner reach the land ahead.

To be possessed of faith is like a man having eyes; to be possessed of a vow is like the light of sun, moon, and lamp. Only when the eyes are lit by the light can they make the road out clearly, and only then can the practitioner reach the destination.
Therefore, if a person who recites the Buddha's name does not make a vow to be reborn there, though he have accomplishment, it all comes to nothing, because he does not comply with the Buddha.
Therefore, if one who recites the Buddha's name does not make the vow of rebirth, even though there be accomplishment, it is all in vain, because one does not follow the Buddha's teaching.
Now you departed spirits should understand this meaning.
Now you departed spirits ought to know this principle.

blocks.text: The First Instruction: Forgoing the False and Returning to the True

inline.s: A hundred thousand leagues do not part us by a grain of dust; cease to make the near and far by delusion and awakening,
In an instant, when the thought is spent and Buddhas countless as the Ganges sand are gone, one is even then a person in the Lotus Land.

[A hundred thousand leagues do not part us by a grain of dust] The Land of Bliss is distant from here by a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands, yet in truth there is not so much as a grain of dust between. This is what was said in the preceding instruction:
“The Pure Land is this very place, and this very place is the Pure Land.”

Ordinary beings fail to realize it only because their minds are deluded. Hence the next line: “Cease to make the near and far by delusion and awakening.” [Cease to make near and far by delusion and awakening] When deluded, the Land of Bliss is a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands away (far); when awakened, this very place is the Land of Bliss (near). [In an instant, when the thought is spent and Buddhas countless as the Ganges sand are gone] When the recitation reaches the point where both subject and object are extinguished, that is the instant in which one has exhausted Buddhas as countless as the sands of the Ganges. [One is even then a person in the Lotus Land] At that very moment one is in the Western Land of Bliss.

To cleave to the dust and turn from awakening is to plant thorns and brambles in a garden of seven jewels; to forgo the false and return to the true is to hang a web of pearls at the gateways of the four modes of birth.

To cleave to the dust and turn from awakening is therefore to plant brambles in a garden of seven jewels (a metaphor for turning this very Land of Bliss into the Saha world); to forgo the false and return to the true is therefore to hang a precious jeweled net at the portals of the four modes of birth (
womb-birth, egg-birth, moisture-birth, transformation-birth
) (a metaphor for restoring this Saha world to the Land of Bliss).

[Cleaving to the dust and turning from awakening] Dust denotes all the worldly dharmas whose defilements stain the true nature; awakening is the intrinsic awareness of sentient beings. “Cleaving to the dust and turning from awakening” means sinking into the dust-realms and turning away from one's intrinsic awareness. [The jeweled net] The precious and exquisite nets of the Land of Bliss.

Woven through all dharmas, and enfolded within a single mind. Where no thinking occurs, Amitabha Buddha cuts off the six root-faculties; where no fabrication is made, the homeland of purity swallows up the eight confines.

The vast array of things is all within the mind (a single mind enfolds the woven-through dharmas). In the place beyond thought (free of deliberation), recite Amitabha Buddha, and sever the six root-faculties (so that the six faculties no longer cling to the six dusts); when nothing is fabricated, the Western Land of Bliss (the homeland of purity) pervades the whole universe.
[Enfolded within a single mind] This is an inverted construction, used for emphasis. [The eight confines] The eight furthest regions of the world.

It breaks the mass of torpor as the bright sun rides the sky; it cures every illness as the good-seen divine medicine. Therefore it is said: one utterance of the name Amitabha Buddha can extinguish the myriad suffering of birth-and-death for eighteen hundred thousand kotis of kalpas.

It breaks the darkness of sentient beings as the bright sun hangs in the sky; it heals all diseases as the medicine-king good-appearance. Therefore it is said: one recitation of the name Amitabha Buddha can wipe away the myriad sufferings of birth and death for eighteen hundred thousand kotis of kalpas.
[Gao (
gǎo
) sun riding the sky] The bright sun illuminating the heavens. [The good-seen divine medicine] That is, the medicine-king good-appearance, the name
of a wondrous medicine. The Avatamsaka Sutra says:

“For example, on the snow mountain there is a great medicine-king named Good-Appearance. Whoever sees it gains pure eyes; whoever hears it gains pure ears; whoever smells its fragrance gains a pure nose; whoever tastes it gains a pure tongue; whoever touches it gains a pure body. And whoever takes the earth of that place is able to extinguish immeasurable illnesses and dwell in peace and joy.”
Such are its benefits — how can simile and speech reach them? Just look at this present third-period recitation rite.

The benefit of reciting the Buddha's name is thus supremely blessed (one utterance of the name Amitabha Buddha can extinguish the myriad suffering of birth-and-death for eighteen hundred thousand kotis of kalpas); how could simile and discourse possibly describe it? Such is the benefit of the present third-period recitation rite — how great it is!
Let me ask: as to this present assembly, the line that we all recite with one voice — how shall it be set forth?
Now, let everyone summarize all that has been said above in a single sentence. How should that sentence be phrased?
Once the Buddha is recited from the root of the tongue, unawares the lotus blossoms beneath the feet.
Utter Amitabha Buddha in a single thought, and unawares a precious lotus blossoms beneath the feet.
[Precious lotus] The Immeasurable Life Sutra says:
“Precious lotus-flowers
(blossoms)
fill the whole world.”

blocks.text: The Second Instruction: A Clear Pearl Clarifies the Water

inline.s: Break open the void, and laughter fills the cheeks; the rare and shimmering treasure-house opens at once,
Even the matter before the empty kalpa is at last contained in the six-syllable sacred name.

Break open the void and rejoice through all of life (laughter fills the cheeks); the intrinsic nature appears entirely (the rare treasure-house opens suddenly); even such a great matter as seeing one's original face (the matter before the empty kalpa) is accomplished by holding to the name and reciting the Buddha (the six-syllable sacred name at last embraces it).
This is the state of having entered the samadhi of Buddha-recitation and of awakening the mind and seeing the nature.
[Straight through]
Even if.
Empty kalpa
One of the four kalpas; the period in which, after this world has been destroyed, only empty space remains.
The four kalpas

Within a single great kalpa there are four intermediate kalpas — the kalpa of formation, the kalpa of abiding, the kalpa of destruction, and the kalpa of emptiness — and each intermediate kalpa in turn contains twenty small kalpas. So-called “formation” means the world being brought together by the assembly of many conditions; “abiding” means sentient beings dwelling in peace, with plants and animals, with borders and history; “destruction” means the beginning of ruin: in the first nineteen small kalpas all plants and animals are destroyed, and in the last small kalpa the land-world upon which sentient beings rely is destroyed; “emptiness” means that once destruction is complete all becomes empty space. The world thus ceaselessly forms, abides, destroys, and empties, again and again.
[The matter before the empty kalpa] Seeing one's original face.
The ancients said: cast a clear pearl into muddy water, and the muddy water cannot but become clear; cast Buddha-recitation into a confused mind, and the confused mind cannot but become Buddha.

The ancients said: cast a clear pearl into muddy water, and the muddy water will certainly become clear; cast recitation of the Buddha's name into a confused mind, and the confused mind will certainly become pure, the thought of recitation never apart from the Buddha.

In the western lands there is a treasure called the clear pearl. It is said that when this pearl is cast into muddy water, for every inch it enters the water, one inch of the muddy water immediately becomes clear. As the pearl descends, from inch to foot, all the way to the bottom, the muddy water likewise becomes clear and still along with it. One should know that the clear pearl is a metaphor for the pure thought of Buddha-recitation; the muddy water is a metaphor for the confused and deluded mind.

In the western lands there is a treasure called the clear pearl. Because this pearl, once cast into muddy water, clarifies one inch for every inch it enters, and from inch to foot all the way to the bottom the muddy water becomes pure along with it, one should know that the clear pearl is a metaphor for the pure thought of recitation, and the muddy water a metaphor for the confused, deluded mind.

At the very moment when the deluded mind is confused and disordered, if one can raise a single thought, as if facing the compassionate one, and hold fast to the six-syllable sacred name, each syllable leaving the mouth and entering the ear, then this confusion of itself grows still along with the thought.

At the moment when the deluded mind is confused and disordered, if one can raise a single thought, as though facing Amitabha Buddha, and recite the six-syllable sacred name (Namo Amitabha Buddha), each syllable leaving the mouth and entering the ear (heard with perfect clarity), then this disorder of itself becomes still along with the thought of recitation.
From this single thought one passes to ten thoughts, and onward until thought after thought does not waver — this is what the teachings call the unbroken succession of pure thoughts.

From this one thought one goes to ten thoughts, until thought upon thought is a thought of recitation — this is what the scriptural teachings call the succession of pure thoughts without interruption (not broken by deluded thoughts).

One who recites the Buddha's name must be earnest in faith and vigorous in the right cause. Reflect again and again upon the sorrow of revolving in birth and death, and deeply detest the turmoil of dust and toil as a sore affliction.

One who recites the Buddha's name must be sincere in faith and resolute in the right cause. Think again and again of the grief of revolving in birth and death, and deeply loathe the turmoil of the dusty world as a source of pain.

Raise the sound of the Buddha's name, and straightway there is no other view. Like the Taie sword, laid level before the hall; like a great wheel of fire, its sparks leaping and its flames blazing. Whatever it brushes is burned, whatever it touches is wounded. Until, at last, the mind is single, not confused, and both subject and object are forgotten.

Raise the sound of the Buddha's name, and straightway there is no other thought. Like the Taie sword, held level before the hall; like a great wheel of fire, its sparks flying and its huge flames blazing. Whatever it brushes (
yīng
, grazes) is scorched away, whatever it touches is wounded. Until at last the mind is single and unconfused, and both subject and object are extinguished.

[Like the Taie sword, laid level before the hall] As one hand grasps the peerlessly sharp Taie sword and the other presses the crossbar at the front of the chariot, leading the whole army to charge the enemy (here the “enemy” is deluded thought and habitual tendencies). [A single mind, unconfused] This is the state in which ten thousand thoughts return to one, and only the thought of recitation remains. [Both subject and object forgotten] Both subject (the mind that recites) and object (the Buddha-name recited) are extinguished. Here “forgotten” is a variant of “annihilated.” For how to reach a single mind unconfused and both subject and object extinguished, see
Inquiry into Buddha-Recitation
As for words of having arrived home, need not be spoken again; as for talk of a shortcut, why trouble the lips with it?
When the work has reached this stage (
“a single mind, unconfused; both subject and object forgotten”

), the saying of having arrived home (rebirth in the Western Land of Bliss) need not be raised again (for birth in the highest grade is already assured); the talk of a shortcut need not be mentioned (for birth in the highest grade is already assured).

It may be called: the very proof of the sacred art of cultivation, surpassing the right path of expedient means; a thunderbolt that splits the hibernating lair of death, a sun and moon that light the dark byways of delusion.

It may be said: the very attestation of the sacred power of cultivation, surpassing the upright path of expediencies; a thunderbolt that bursts the cavern of death's hibernation, a sun and moon that illumine the dark roads of delusion.
[Hibernating lair (
zhé
)] The cave where hibernating insects lie hidden. [Hibernating insects] The creatures that hide in the earth for the winter (
zhì
). [Byway (
qú
)] A highway.
Tonight the three-period recitation rite is drawing to its close; the many departed spirits upon the hall of rebirth, receiving this supreme goodness, are assured of rebirth.

Tonight the three-period recitation rite is about to be completed; the many departed spirits upon the hall of rebirth, receiving this supreme virtue, are certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Bliss.
Let me ask: before a single thought has sprouted, is there still this tidings or not?
Let me ask: before a single thought has sprouted, is there still any tidings? (The answer is the following verse.)
Since the mind is empty and still, on what does the thought rely? The homeland of old says “return” — who has not yet returned?
Beyond the blossoms, a jade cock crows the dawning sun; afar it welcomes the new Buddha, attending the compassionate majesty.

This mind being empty and still, how can deluded thoughts cling to it? The homeland of old (the Land of Bliss) says to return — why have you not yet returned? Beyond the blossoms the jade cock crows the dawn (the daybreak is a metaphor for the time of rebirth having arrived), and at the command of Amitabha Buddha it goes afar to welcome the new Buddha.
[The new Buddha] Refers to the newly arrived reborn one. Because one who is reborn in the Western Land of Bliss attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime, they are called a new Buddha.

blocks.text: The Third Instruction: Partaking of the Buddha's Realization

inline.s: Now that the recitation of the Buddha's name arises from the mind, how could the binding of karma come from without? In a moment of turning from the mind of recitation, that very instant is the place where karma is bound.

Since recitation of the Buddha's name arises from the mind, how could the making of karma belong to what is external? In an instant of turning from the mind of recitation, that very moment is the place where karma is formed.
[Bound karma] Thoughts and actions that arise from affliction.

Now this assembly, relying upon the teaching, performs the three-period recitation rite. The supreme causes gathered are especially for the many departed spirits upon the hall of rebirth, that they may be surely reborn in the Pure Land.

Today the great assembly of the Dharma gathering, relying upon the teaching, performs the three-period recitation rite. The supreme causes thus gathered are especially for the many departed spirits upon the hall of rebirth, that they may be certain of rebirth in the Western Land of Bliss.

From now the fragrance of precepts is rich, the torch of wisdom burns bright. The clouds of delusion part, and the sky of one's nature stands alone bright; the dust of falsehood is exhausted, and the ground of the mind opens broad and clear. All the faculties are fully pure, and the host of karma is at once emptied.

Today the fragrance of precepts is rich (an intense fragrance), the torch of wisdom is brilliant (radiant). The clouds of delusion clear, and the sky of one's nature shines alone; the dust of falsehood is spent, and the ground of the mind opens wide (clear and bright). The six faculties are wholly pure, and the host of karmas is instantly emptied.
Raise a single thought, and a single flower opens, drawing the dew
yì
to the wind, its fragrance floating over the jeweled pool; let a single emotion run free, and a single fruit ripens, wrapped in smoke against the sun, its shadow falling on the golden garden.

Utter the name of the Buddha once, and a single lotus opens, drawing dew to meet the wind, its fragrance drifting over the precious pool; let emotion go once, and a single fruit of karma ripens, veiling the sun with smoke, falling as a shade upon the heart's field.

[Let a single emotion run free] To give free rein once to emotional consciousness. [Wrapped in smoke against the sun] Smoke obscuring the sun; a metaphor for turning away from Amitabha Buddha through delusion. [Falling on the golden garden] The shadow-images of the six dusts (the illusory reflections of clinging to the six dusts) spread over the mind.

Walking, standing, sitting, and lying are all within it; roaming and sport are no matter apart. Partaking of the Buddha's realization, one reaches the very bottom of the Dharma source. The ground of eternal stillness and light appears everywhere, and the great king of vows meets in every speck of dust.

Walking, standing, sitting, and lying are all within it; roaming and enjoying are not a matter apart. Partaking of the Buddha's realization, one penetrates to the root of the Dharma. The ground of eternal stillness and light manifests before one at every place, and the ten great king of vows joins in every particle of dust.
This is the state of having realized “mind-only Pure Land, self-nature Amitabha.”
[The ground of eternal stillness and light] This is the land of eternal stillness and light, one of the four lands. [The four lands]

That is, the land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, the land of expedient remaining, the land of real reward and adornment, and the land of eternal stillness and light. The land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together is the land where ordinary beings live together with sages who manifest bodies and expound the Dharma in order to convert them; the land of expedient remaining is the land of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the Dharma-body; the land of real reward and adornment is the land of the Buddha's reward-body and the bodhisattvas on the grounds; the land of eternal stillness and light is the land shown in the stillness of the Buddha's pure Dharma-body. [The great king of vows] The ten great vows of Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) Bodhisattva: first, to reverence all Buddhas; second, to praise the Tathagata; third, to make abundant offerings; fourth, to repent karmic hindrances; fifth, to rejoice in others' merit; sixth, to request the turning of the Dharma-wheel; seventh, to request the Buddha to remain in the world; eighth, to follow the Buddha's teaching always; ninth, to accord with sentient beings always; tenth, to dedicate all merit universally. [The ten great king of vows meets in every speck of dust] In the most subtle of every point, one accords with the ten great king of vows.
Once more, on behalf of the departed spirits, with utmost sincerity we repent and make our vows.
Once more, on behalf of the departed spirits of this hall, with utmost sincerity we repent and make our vows.

blocks.text: Fourth Exhortation: Forever Depart from the Sea of Karma

inline.s: Throughout the three periods of mindfulness just observed, we have called upon the vast and virtuous name of Amitabha Buddha, urging the departed spirits of this hall to repent their accumulated karma and vow to be reborn. Since their practice and vows are deep, their merit is not wasted.

Throughout the three periods of mindfulness from the very outset, [we call upon] the vast and virtuous name of Amitabha Buddha, urging the departed spirits of this hall to repent the karma they have created and vow to be reborn. Since their practice and vows are deep, their merit is not wasted.

We only pray that the departed spirits, hearing this essential Dharma, will believe, accept, and practice it. From this moment they will take up their bodies in the lotus womb, forever depart from the sea of karma, directly realize the stage of no-retrogression, and perfect the supreme bodhi without remainder.

We only pray that the departed spirits, hearing this essential Dharma, will believe, accept, and practice it. Thereupon they will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, forever depart from the sea of karma, directly realize the stage of no-retrogression, and perfect the supreme bodhi (attain Buddhahood).

[Tuo zhi: to lodge one’s body.] [Lotus womb: those reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss through reciting the Buddha’s name are all born by transformation within a lotus; because the lotus resembles a mother’s womb, it is called the ‘lotus womb.’] [A-bi (
pi

) ba-zhi: the stage of no-retrogression.] This is the name of a bodhisattva stage; a bodhisattva must pass through a great asamkhya kalpa of practice before reaching this stage. From here on one advances only step by step until Buddhahood, with no turning back in between. The Buddha Speaks the Amitabha Sutra says:
“Sentient beings born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all avivartika (never retrogressive).”
